title: 🕊️ UN agrees to draft rules for "killer robots" by 2028 — with no binding commitment!
body: 🕊️ UN agrees to draft rules for "killer robots" by 2028 — with no binding commitment!

Member states of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons agreed to develop an international document on lethal autonomous weapons systems, known as "killer robots", within two years, after talks in Geneva that ended in the early hours of Saturday, November 21.

But the agreement did not specify whether the new document will be legally binding or not: the delegations agreed on the word "drafting" instead of "negotiating" for the next stage, in a watered-down formulation that left the most important question open.

Around 100 countries supported legally binding rules within a short timeframe, to regulate weapons systems that select and attack targets with varying degrees of independence from humans, but major arms-producing countries such as the United States, Russia and Israel opposed that.

Seven countries, including Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama, proposed starting negotiations towards a legally binding protocol, while the United States proposed a five-year mandate to draw up non-binding guidelines on applying international humanitarian law to these weapons.

The conference, the seventh review conference of the convention, was held in Geneva from November 16 to 20, with 128 member states taking part, amid growing concern about the use of lethal autonomous weapons in conflicts, including Ukraine, Sudan and the Middle East.

The UN Secretary-General, the Pope and the International Committee of the Red Cross had all called for strong, legally binding rules, and the Secretary-General set a deadline of the end of 2026 to start negotiations, as he leaves office at the end of the year.

The "Stop Killer Robots" coalition criticised the final agreement, saying a small number of countries weakened the mandate despite broad support for binding rules, while the conference president, Swiss Ambassador Julien Toni, described it as an important achievement after more than ten years of talks.
Human Rights Watch also noted that 163 countries voted for a UN General Assembly resolution supporting the creation of legally binding rules on these weapons.

Simply put: the world agreed to spend two more years talking about "killer robots" without yet deciding whether it will actually ban them. The machine that kills without humans still has no binding rules.
Should the decision to kill always remain in human hands, or does the machine have a role on the battlefield?
